summary: Every one of the eight claims made to me landed in the staged bytes -- I checked each against `git show :<path>` rather than the launcher's account, and none is missing. My round-3 major (R3a) is genuinely discharged: the answer-from-the-pointer mutation is dead, because the ADR now requires the pointed delta to carry that exact (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq) and the discriminating test I named at round 3 -- commit 5 and 6 in SEPARATE deltas, replay 5, assert not 6's firstOffset -- now fails against it. All three discriminating tests still hold unchanged, and R3b/R3d are discharged outright while R3c is half-discharged. The new defect is not in the rule but in the two sentences that justify it. The refuse branch is reached by TWO cases the sequencer cannot tell apart -- a genuine replay of a flush that DID apply in an older delta, and a HOLE (flushSeq consumed by a commit that threw; DefaultIngest.java:349 increments through the throw) where nothing applied -- and the ADR asserts the hole's semantics for the whole branch: 'nothing applied under that key, and the caller can re-flush'. In the case the paragraph is actually about, the key applied and re-flushing commits those records a SECOND time, which this ADR's own Consequences explains ('a producer-level retry is a NEW flush under a new key -- not a replay at all') and which is the harm FR-3 exists to prevent. M4.10d's standing note says the opposite again from the other side: skip-and-return 'turns a landed flush into a producer-visible failure', a defect M4.10's own review recorded. So the implementer gets three documents disagreeing about what a refusal means to the caller, with the accepted ADR the loudest and the wrong one. One deletion repairs it, and an argued baselines line is an equally valid disposition.

findings.title: THE REFUSAL'S SAFETY CLAIM IS FALSE IN THE CASE THE PARAGRAPH IS ABOUT, and the caller action it prescribes is the duplicate FR-3 exists to prevent
findings.failure_scenario: l.69-70: 'Refusing neither duplicates nor suppresses: nothing applied under that key, and the caller can re-flush.' The refuse branch is entered when flushSeq <= lastAppliedFlushSeq for the SAME incarnation and the pointed delta does not carry that flushSeq. Two distinct histories reach it and the sequencer cannot tell them apart. (i) THE CASE THE PARAGRAPH OPENS WITH -- 'two flushes committed in separate batches sit in separate deltas' -- pod A commits (I,5) into delta 100 and (I,6) into delta 101, slot points at 101, a duplicate of 5 arrives. Flush 5 APPLIED. 'Nothing applied under that key' is simply false here, and 'the caller can re-flush' commits flush 5's records a second time at fresh offsets: a duplicate, which this same ADR's Consequences explains in full ('DefaultIngest.flushLocked ... a producer-level retry is a NEW flush under a new key with an incremented flushSeq -- not a replay at all'). (ii) A HOLE: flush 5's commit throws, flush 6 lands. DefaultIngest.java:349 is `new CommitRequest(podShortId, flushSeq++, ...)`, so the number is consumed whether or not the commit lands -- flushSeq is dense over ISSUED flushes, not over APPLIED ones, which is the density l.53 asserts. lastApplied=6 with no 5, so a later retry of 5 is MISREAD as a replay and refused, suppressing a real commit -- the harm this ADR names as worse than duplication. In (ii) the sentence is true; in (i) it is false; the branch is the same branch. The ADR states (ii)'s semantics as if they were the branch's. Meanwhile backlog-notes.md M4.10d, unchanged by this commit, tells the implementer the opposite for (i): 'Skip-and-return satisfies "refuse", but Sequencer defines the return as what a caller matches by its submitted segment key and DefaultIngest then completes the append exceptionally: a retry after an ambiguous IOException ... becomes a producer-visible failure on a flush that LANDED' -- a defect the M4.10 review recorded and the baselines entry still quotes. Reachability in M4 production is nil (flushLocked holds one lock, so a commit-level retry is always depth one and the pointer always matches), which is precisely what makes it dangerous: it is M4-invisible and it is what M5's forwarded, reordered or concurrent commits meet first -- the same shape that disqualified the lease epoch at l.19-22 and that the per-SegmentCommit clause was added to prevent.
findings.mutation_that_survives: M4.10d implements the refusal exactly as prescribed and adds the caller half the ADR authorises: on refusal, DefaultIngest re-flushes. The test written from this prose -- 'refuse an unanswerable replay, then assert the re-flush succeeds' -- is GREEN while one set of records now holds two sets of committed offsets. Nothing in the ADR, in M4.10d's row or in its notes requires the assertion that kills it (that the re-flushed records are not the refused flush's records, or that a refusal is NOT presented to a caller as retryable), and no fixture anywhere distinguishes case (i) from case (ii), so an implementation that treats every refusal as (ii) passes everything. The second, cheaper mutation: never enter the answer path at all -- always refuse a detected replay -- which contradicts only the row, not this paragraph.
findings.remedy: DELETE the justification, do not rewrite it: 'Refusing neither duplicates nor suppresses: nothing applied under that key, and the caller can re-flush.' The rule above it stands without it. The tree's own recorded pattern for this failure is deletion -- baselines/review.txt rounds:M4.10a, 'three false claims of mine, all deleted rather than rewritten ... a deletion cannot add a claim', and rounds:M4.10, 'every fix added a REASON beside the correction, and the reason was the next round's finding'. If a sentence is wanted in its place, the only one that is true of both cases is that the sequencer cannot tell an applied-but-unanswerable flush from a never-applied one, and M4.10d owns which way that resolves. An argued `rounds:`-style line in the staged baselines/review.txt discharging this as M4.10d's to settle is an equally valid disposition under review.md `fixed-or-argued`; it is the CLAIM I am blocking on, not the choice to refuse.

findings.title: 'a distinguishable error' names no observable, and the only channel this seam has means the opposite
findings.failure_scenario: You asked whether a test can enforce it. Not as written: 'distinguishable' names neither what it is distinguishable FROM nor by what observable. Sequencer.commit returns CommitDelta or throws IOException, and nothing else -- a lost CAS race deliberately never surfaces (Sequencer.java javadoc, ADR-0022). IOException on this seam is documented as 'the store was unreachable -- AMBIGUOUS, so the commit may or may not have landed. Retrying with the same (podId, flushSeq) is safe only from M4.10'. So the one available channel carries the meaning RETRY THIS EXACT KEY, which is the one thing a refused caller must not do: the retry re-enters the same branch and is refused again. The ADR's own framing -- 'nothing that changes meaning when M5 moves the sequencer out of process' -- is the argument for naming the observable here, since at M5 a refusal has to cross a wire as something other than a transport error.
findings.mutation_that_survives: Implement the refusal as `throw new IOException("replay not answerable")`. It is refused; it is an error; the message distinguishes it. Every assertion derivable from this ADR passes, including `assertThatThrownBy(...).isInstanceOf(IOException.class)`. Killed only by an assertion on a type or an outcome variant that the ADR does not name, so nobody is required to write it. Same blast radius as R4a; recorded separately because the remedy is different -- one clause naming the observable, or one clause handing the signal to M4.10d and saying plainly it must not be IOException.
findings.remedy: Either name it ('a distinct exception, never IOException, which this seam defines as ambiguous-and-retryable') or hand it to M4.10d in the same words. Not worth a round on its own; it rides on R4a's fix.

findings.title: The pointer reached three surfaces and missed the fourth -- Consequences still amends ADR-0033 with the incarnation alone
findings.failure_scenario: Verified the claim: the pointer DID land in 'Which formats change' (l.92-96), in ADR-0033's own banner ('gains an incarnationId and a pointer to the delta that last applied') and in M4.10c's row. It did not land in this ADR's own Consequences paragraph, l.152-155: 'its per-pod lastAppliedFlushSeq gains an incarnationId beside it', full stop. That is now the one restatement of the amendment that is short by a field. Harm is bounded -- it is a status paragraph about ADR-0033, not a section anyone encodes from, and the two surfaces a session encodes from both carry the pointer -- which is why this is minor and not R3a's shape repeated.
findings.mutation_that_survives: None -- documentation consistency, no behaviour rides on it.
findings.remedy: Four words, or nothing. ⚠️ MY RECOMMENDATION IS NOTHING: per review.md `minors-land`, and because the surface a fix creates is exactly what has bought the last two rounds here. Record it in the commit body.

findings.title: The answer-or-refuse rule landed in the ADR and not in the row the implementer works from
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10d's row still reads 'a replay is flushSeq <= lastApplied for the same incarnation, answered with the ORIGINAL offsets' -- no match condition, no refuse branch. That sentence is fully satisfied by the R3a mutation (answer from the slot's pointer without checking its flushSeq), and its notes add nothing on this axis: the new 'PIN THE UPDATE RULE' paragraph is about the merge, not about answerability. What saves it is that both the row and the note say 'per ADR-0036' by name, and the ADR is now unambiguous -- so a session that opens the cited ADR cannot get this wrong. That is the whole distance between this and a major.
findings.mutation_that_survives: Answer any detected replay from the pointed delta's SegmentCommit for that pod without matching flushSeq. Green against the row as written and against every fixture the notes require, all of which are depth one. Dead the moment the ADR is read, which the row instructs.
findings.remedy: Six words in the row if it is touched for another reason: 'answered from the pointed delta or refused'. Not worth a round; not worth a fix on its own.

findings.title: The size number is now right and still measures nothing -- carried from R3c, half discharged
findings.failure_scenario: Verified: '16 bytes as a UUID and the pointer two longs, about 32 bytes per pod' is arithmetically correct and the stale 16 is gone from the conclusion, which was the substance of R3c. Two halves of R3c survive, both pre-existing: the heading still says 'grows by fixed-width fields per pod' while Checkpoint.encode writes the pods map with putUvarint (Checkpoint.java:137), and the assertion the paragraph argues from -- CheckpointTest's isLessThan(64*1024) -- puts exactly ONE pod in its fixture, so it is blind to per-pod width at any value. The arithmetic is standing in for a measurement, on the axis ADR-0033's size argument is amended against.
findings.mutation_that_survives: Widen the per-pod slot to any size at all -- 32 bytes, 256, MAX_KEY_BYTES: the cited assertion is green, because the fixture has one pod. That is the finding, not a kill.
findings.remedy: Let M4.10c's row own a pods-dimension size assertion when it changes the encoding. Nothing to do in this commit.

what_i_verified: Staged hash: `git diff --cached | sha256sum` = 5584bcc57e7c164b52a0d4b8c3baeb604f32003a253029798a5ad92af711c895, matches the packet and the hash I was told to carry.

CLAIM CHECK, against `git show :<path>` and not the account given to me -- ALL EIGHT LANDED. (1) answer-only-on-exact-triple plus refuse-otherwise plus the M4.46 reason: ADR l.60-70, present. (2) incarnation UNORDERED with the slot-overwrite bound: l.72-81, present, and it is a real bound, naming X(Ix,5)/Y(Iy,3) and the foreign watermark. (3) 'Which formats change' carries the pointer: l.92-96, present, with an explicit 'normative HERE, not only in Consequences'. (4) ADR-0033's banner: staged 0033 line 7 reads 'gains an incarnationId and a pointer to the delta that last applied', present. (5) M4.10c's row: backlog.md:123 carries '(incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq, epoch, sequence) -- watermark AND pointer', present. (6) archive row says INGESTER: backlog-done.md:149, present. (7) '~32 bytes per pod': l.138-140, present and arithmetically right. (8) 175/200 caveated as a fixture artifact: l.27-30 and the M4.46 note, present, and the figure is removed from the archive row rather than restated. Nothing I was told is in the diff is missing from it.

R3a IS DISCHARGED, and I verified it by re-running my own round-3 mutation against the new prose rather than against the summary. The mutation was 'answer a detected replay from the slot's pointer without checking that its flushSeq equals the replayed one'. l.64-66 now forbids it in words a test can be written from -- 'read the pointed delta and answer only if it carries that exact (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq)' -- and the discriminating fixture I named at round 3 (commit (podA,I,5) and (podA,I,6) in SEPARATE deltas, replay 5) now has a required outcome that the mutation fails: not 6's firstOffset. The fixture is constructible at T0 today: two sequential commits produce two deltas, and BatchingSequencer merges only concurrent ones.

R3b IS DISCHARGED: the forward reference at l.159 ('the slot-overwrite bound above') now resolves -- grep for overwrit|destruct|interleav|unordered over the ADR returns l.72-81 as well as the reference, where at round 3 it returned only the reference.
R3d IS DISCHARGED: backlog-done.md:149 no longer says 'per producer process'.

DISCRIMINATING TEST #1 (minting) HOLDS UNCHANGED. l.36-47 is byte-identical to the round-3 text: 'minted once per INGESTER process -- the same object that mints flushSeq, i.e. one per DefaultIngest instance', with the per-flush mutation named and IngestCommitPathTest's Recording decorator identified as the seam that sees it. DefaultIngest.java:63 (`private long flushSeq` instance field) and :349 (the sole issuance site) still hold, so the clause is still true of the tree.

DISCRIMINATING TEST #2 (per-SegmentCommit placement) HOLDS UNCHANGED, and its row-level gap from R3e is now CLOSED: M4.10c's row itself carries 'PER SegmentCommit, not once per delta: every M4 delta is single-segment so the two placements are byte-equivalent today and only M5 tells them apart'. The two-pod fixture that kills the once-per-delta mutation still exists at BatchingSequencerTest.java:259.

DISCRIMINATING TEST #3 (the update rule) HOLDS UNCHANGED: backlog-notes.md M4.10d still carries 'PIN THE UPDATE RULE, NOT ONLY THE COMPARISON' over CheckpointWriter's `pods.merge(podId, flushSeq, Math::max)`, and this commit adds the slot-destructibility bound to it.

REFUSING CANNOT BE CONFUSED WITH THE ACCEPT PATH FOR A NEW INCARNATION -- checked directly, as asked. The accept decision is reached before any pointer read: a different incarnationId is accepted (l.57) and never enters the lookup. The mutation that WOULD confuse them (compare flushSeq <= lastApplied while ignoring incarnation, so a restarted pod's flush 0 is detected, found absent from the pointed delta, and refused) is killed by a required fixture: backlog-notes.md M4.10d states 'The killing scenario is a restarted pod reissuing 0 for a NEW segment, which must be ACCEPTED' and 'THE DISCRIMINATOR IS A POD RESTART, NOT A TAKEOVER'. That test must assert acceptance -- offsets assigned -- not merely absence of a duplicate; the note already says so. So this half of your question is sound. The confusion that DOES survive is inside the refuse branch itself, between an applied flush and a hole, which is R4a.

M4.10c's row dropped 'Atomic per non-negotiable 8, ADR travels here' in this commit -- I checked whether that is an instruction getting looser alongside the change, the docs analogue of a weakened assertion. It is not: backlog-notes.md M4.10c still carries 'THE FORMAT ADR TRAVELS IN THIS COMMIT ... wire-format-change requires the record, the codec, every reader and writer, the fakes, the golden and the ADR together', in fuller form than the row ever did, and the row links to it. No finding.
M4.10d's row dropped 'Discriminator is a POD RESTART' in this commit; same check, same answer -- the note carries it in capitals as its own paragraph. No finding.
M4.46 RESOLVES: the ADR cites 'the invariant M4.46 names' and backlog.md:150 is a real todo row stating that invariant, with a note under #m446. The ID names something a reader can hold.

Present-tense claims in the NEW prose check out against the tree: 'two flushes committed in separate batches sit in separate deltas' is true of BatchingSequencer (it merges concurrent commits only); 'The slot holds ONE pointer' is the decision being made, stated as such. The one present-tense claim that does NOT hold is the density the refuse branch leans on -- see R4a, DefaultIngest.java:349 increments flushSeq through a throwing commit.

No code and no tests changed: `git diff --cached --stat` is six documentation files (baselines/review.txt, backlog.md, backlog-done.md, backlog-notes.md, ADR-0033, ADR-0036). Nothing existing was weakened; there is no assertion in this diff to weaken. The `rounds:M4.10b` argument required by review.md `two-round-cap` is present and staged in baselines/review.txt, keyed first field, with a reason.

I did not read the author's reasoning for this round; I read my own round-3 verdict from .harness/review to recover the three discriminating tests I am asked about, and the packet's open-findings list.

answers_to_the_launcher.did_every_claim_you_made_actually_land: Yes -- all eight, checked one at a time against `git show :<path>` rather than against your account, with line numbers in what_i_verified. Nothing you described is absent from the staged bytes. Given round 3, I state that as a measurement and not as a courtesy.
answers_to_the_launcher.do_the_three_discriminating_tests_still_: All three, unchanged, and two are better supported than at round 3: #2's row-level gap (my R3e) is closed by M4.10c's rewritten row, and #3 gained the slot-destructibility bound in M4.10d's note. Nothing this round weakened any of them.
answers_to_the_launcher.does_the_answer_or_refuse_rule_admit_a_m: The rule itself does not -- it kills R3a's mutation cleanly and the depth-two fixture that discriminates it is constructible at T0. Its two JUSTIFYING sentences do. 'Nothing applied under that key, and the caller can re-flush' is true only of the hole case and false of the case the paragraph opens with, where the key applied and re-flushing duplicates; the mutation that survives is the caller half the sentence authorises, tested green. That is R4a and it is what blocks.
answers_to_the_launcher.can_a_test_enforce_distinguishable_error: No, as written. 'Distinguishable' names neither the counterparty nor the observable, and the seam's only failure channel is IOException, documented as ambiguous-and-retry-the-same-key -- the opposite instruction. `throw new IOException("replay not answerable")` survives every assertion the ADR licenses. R4b, minor, because it rides on R4a's fix.
answers_to_the_launcher.can_refusing_be_confused_with_accepting_: Not across that boundary -- accept is decided on the incarnation before the pointer is read, and the mutation that would confuse them is killed by a fixture M4.10d's notes already require in the right direction (a restarted pod's flush 0 must be ACCEPTED, not merely not-duplicated). The confusion is INSIDE the refuse branch: an applied-but-unanswerable flush and a hole from a consumed-but-failed flushSeq are indistinguishable there, and the ADR asserts the hole's semantics for both.
answers_to_the_launcher.is_it_landable: Not as staged, on two sentences -- and the block is on a CLAIM, not on the decision. The key, the minting site, the formats, the placement, the pointer and the answer-or-refuse rule are all sound and all now enforceable; my round-3 major is genuinely dead. What is left is the safety argument attached to the fix, which is the exact habit baselines/review.txt records for this task family: the reason beside the correction becomes the next round's finding. So the cheapest correct disposition is DELETION of the sentence, which cannot add a claim and creates no new surface -- or a staged argued line under review.md `fixed-or-argued` handing the refusal's caller-visible semantics to M4.10d. Either discharges it. R4b through R4e are minors and I recommend fixing none of them.
